t: Aim and plan of the session
n: This laboratory session is devoted to the mineralisation of biological objects. The plan has two parts: first, mineralisation of biological objects with mixtures of sulphuric and nitric acids; second, denitration of the mineralisate and its preparation for analysis. The aim is to introduce the isolation of heavy metal compounds from a biological object by mineralisation, that is, destruction, using sulphuric and nitric acids. The processes of denitration and preparation for analysis are also considered.

Four outcomes are expected from the session. First, to take an object containing metal compounds and study its appearance. Second, to become familiar with detecting oxidants in the mineralisate and removing them chemically with formaldehyde. Third, to prepare the denitrated mineralisate for the detection of metal cations. Fourth, the student who has finished the work has the instructor check the correctness of the results and writes a conclusion in the laboratory notebook.

The apparatus and equipment needed for the work: Kjeldahl flask, stand, gas burner, fume cupboard, reagents, demonstration materials, adhesive tape and paper. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities. For the practical work a 500 ml Kjeldahl flask, a 100 ml beaker and a porcelain dish are needed. The reagents used are a solution of diphenylamine in concentrated H2SO4 and a formaldehyde solution.

t: Metallic poisons change in the body
n: Metallic poisons undergo various changes in the body. PbCO3 or BaCO3 is converted into chlorides in the stomach under the action of acid, converted into carbonates in the intestine, and forms sulphides in the large intestine. Metal compounds are absorbed into the blood mainly in the small intestine; organometallic compounds are absorbed better than inorganic ones. Metals of variable valency are oxidised and reduced: As5+ passes into the more toxic As3+, and metallic mercury into Hg2+.

Metals form complexes with proteins. Mercury, lead, copper, zinc, cadmium, nickel and cobalt form stable coordination compounds, albuminates, with proteins, that is, with peptides or amino acids. The –COOH, –SH and –NH2 groups take part in complex formation, as do nucleic and citric acids and the –OH, –PO3H and –SO3H groups. Free ions leave the blood quickly, while large complexes and colloids are retained in the liver and spleen.

Why is mineralisation needed? To capture metal-containing compounds, they must be converted into the ionic state. For this purpose the object is mineralised, that is, burned, and the metal is brought into the ionic state. Only after that are the cations determined. In 1824 the Russian scientist Nelyubin provided the theoretical basis for the necessity of mineralisation for detecting metallic poisons.

In accordance with the orders of the Ministry of Health on forensic medical examination, testing for 13 metals is necessary. They are distributed by analytical group. From group 2, Ba2+. From group 3, Mn2+, Cr3+, Zn2+ and Tl. From group 4, Pb, Cu, Hg, Cd, Ag and Bi. From group 5, As and Sb. In the table, the group 4 cations are given as Pb2+, Cu2+, Hg2+, Cd2+, Ag+ and Bi3+, and group 5 as As3+, As5+, Sb3+ and Sb5+.

Methods of mineralisation are divided into two groups: dry ashing, and the wet method with various oxidants in an acid medium. Dry methods are particular: they are used for isolating cations of non-volatile metals; these are simple ashing and ashing with added oxidants. H2O2, NH4NO3, HNO3 or HNO3 + H2O2, and NaNO3 + Na2CO3 are used as oxidant. Wet methods are general and are used for isolating all metals except mercury.

Let us look at the history of mineralisation methods. In 1820 Dufléos and Millon worked with chlorine gas. In 1824 Nelyubin put into practice heating the object with "pure" nitric acid until a clear solution was obtained. In 1844 Fresenius and Babo proposed a method using evolved chlorine; the method was used in forensic chemistry for more than 100 years. In 1908 Ravnadix proposed sulphuric and nitric acid, and in 1932 Kahn proposed H2SO4 + HNO3 + HClO4. Later investigations went in two directions: with chlorine, and with various oxidants in the presence of sulphuric acid.

Mineralisation with chlorine is based on the chlorine evolved from KClO3 and HCl. Working with chlorine is convenient mainly for detecting mercury. Its disadvantages: organic substances are destroyed incompletely; a long time is required, 18-20 hours for 100 g of object. In the analysis of arsenic and mercury there are large losses, and the large final volume reduces the sensitivity of the analysis. Chlorine oxidises the organic matter.

t: Sulphuric and nitric acid method: evaluation
n: We evaluate the sulphuric and nitric acid method. The object is oxidised by atomic oxygen evolved from the sulphuric and nitric acids. Its advantages: organic compounds are destroyed completely, relatively little time is needed, and a mineralisate of small volume is obtained. The disadvantage, however, is that almost all the mercury is lost. Remember: this method is not suitable for detecting mercury.

A mixture of sulphuric acid and ammonium nitrate is called the Stepanov and Neumark method. In this method, sulphuric acid forms nitric acid with ammonium nitrate: H2SO4 and 2NH4NO3 give 2HNO3 and (NH4)2SO4. On heating, atomic oxygen is evolved, which oxidises and nitrates the object. A large amount of (NH4)2SO4 salt forms in the mineralisate. Mineralisation proceeds more completely than by the chlorine method, but not to completion.

We compare other acid mixtures. H2SO4 and H2O2, that is, perhydrol, have almost no practical significance: mineralisation is incomplete, and perhydrol is expensive. Its advantage is that no excess nitrogen oxidants remain at the end of the reaction. In 1932 Kahn proposed H2SO4 + HNO3 + HClO4: mineralisation is complete, but perchloric acid gives an extremely dangerous, readily flammable product. The H2SO4 + NH4NO3 mixture is more complete than the chlorine method, but does not go to completion.

The sequence for starting mineralisation. The comminuted object, 100 g, is placed in a 500 ml Kjeldahl flask. 75 ml of a mixture consisting of equal parts of concentrated H2SO4, HNO3 and water is added. The flask is fixed in the stand rather high above the gas flame and heated carefully. When it darkens, HNO3 (1:1) is added.

In the first stage of mineralisation, the "formed" elements of the object, that is, the connective tissues, dissolve in the liquid inside the flask. When destroying objects that are not rich in fat, this process lasts 20-30 minutes. After the formed elements have been destroyed, the flask is lowered closer to the flame and the temperature is raised. With this, the second stage is entered.

The second stage of mineralisation. After the formed elements have been destroyed, the flask is lowered closer to the flame and the temperature is raised. The mineralisate gradually begins to darken; this means that the second stage has begun and that the oxidant is insufficient. Carefully, dropwise, an aqueous solution of nitric acid at a 1:1 ratio is added until the dark colour disappears. This process is continued until mineralisation is complete.

t: How to tell that mineralisation is complete
n: How do we know that mineralisation is complete? If no darkening occurs when the mineralisate is heated for 30 minutes without adding oxidant, the process is considered complete. At this point white heavy vapours of sulphur(VI) oxide are evolved. In mineralisation, it is required to explain by chemical reactions the destruction of organic molecules by oxidants.

We summarise the stages of mineralisation. In the first stage the formed elements dissolve; for this the mixture is heated for 20-30 minutes. In the second stage the mineralisate darkens, which indicates a lack of oxidant, and HNO3 (1:1) is added dropwise. Sign of completion: white heavy SO3 vapours are evolved and there is no darkening for 30 minutes.

t: Freeing from oxidants: dechlorination and denitration
n: Oxidants interfere with the analysis of arsenic and lead and with precipitation as sulphides, so the wet mineralisate is freed from them. Dechlorination is used when mineralising with chlorine: water is added at 5-6 times the volume and evaporated on a 50 °C water bath until HCl ≈ 2%; it is tested with starch-iodide paper, and 12-13 hours are needed, or 2-3 hours with air. Denitration is used when mineralising in the presence of nitric acid or its salts; HNO3, HNO2 and nitrogen oxides are removed, the most difficult being nitrosyl sulphuric acid.

Detecting oxidants in the mineralisate. 1-2 drops of cooled mineralisate are placed in a porcelain dish and the same amount of water is added. To the mixture, 1-2 drops of a solution of diphenylamine in concentrated sulphuric acid are added. If there are oxidants in the mineralisate, the mixture turns blue. Thus, a blue colour shows the presence of an oxidant.

The sequence for denitration with formaldehyde. The mineralisate is carefully transferred from the Kjeldahl flask into a 100 ml beaker containing 10-15 ml of water. It is heated slowly to boiling while formaldehyde solution is added dropwise. Sometimes a brown gas is evolved; it is required to explain the name of the substance with an equation. When gas evolution has ceased, the liquid is boiled for 1-2 minutes.

Checking that denitration is complete. When gas evolution has ceased, the liquid is boiled for 1-2 minutes and tested again for oxidants with diphenylamine solution. If the reaction is positive, another 1-2 drops of formaldehyde are added to the mineralisate and it is heated. The process is continued until no colour forms on testing with diphenylamine.

Nitrosyl sulphuric acid. In mineralisation in the presence of nitric acid, this is the oxidant that is hardest to remove. In pure form it is a colourless crystalline substance melting at 70 °C; in moist air and in water it hydrolyses quickly, giving H2SO4 and HNO2. It usually forms when the sulphuric acid concentration is above 57.5%. To remove it, the mineralisate is diluted.

t: Denitration: hydrolysis and the chemical method
n: We compare two methods of denitration. In the hydrolytic method, the mineralisate is diluted with 5-10 parts of distilled water and evaporated until white sulphur dioxide anhydride forms; this requires 9-17 hours. Chemical methods convert the oxidants into readily volatile gaseous substances and drive them off; this takes 5-10 minutes. Formaldehyde, sulphite, urea or an ammonium salt is used as reagent. The mineralisate freed from oxidants is diluted to 180 ml and boiled.

Removing excess formaldehyde. When denitration is complete, the mineralisate is heated for 5 minutes to remove excess formaldehyde. After that the mineralisate is diluted to 180 ml and boiled for 5 minutes. The task is set of writing the chemical equation of this method.

t: Preparing the mineralisate for further analysis
n: Preparing the mineralisate for further analysis. The mineralisate obtained is diluted with purified water to a volume of 180 ml. It is boiled for 5 minutes and left until the next session. In the next session, laboratory work no. 10, a precipitate is separated from the mineralisate and barium and lead are analysed in it.

Chemical methods of denitration. The task from the book is as follows: name the chemical methods of denitration and write their reactions. Reaction with formaldehyde: 4HNO3 + 3CH2O → 4NO + 3CO2 + 5H2O. With sodium sulphite: Na2SO3 + H2SO4 → Na2SO4 + H2SO3, then H2SO3 → H2O + SO2. The name of the fourth method is left blank; its reaction is: (NH4)2SO4 + 2HNO3 → 2N2O + H2SO4 + 4H2O.

t: Basics of masking in the fractional method
n: Basics of masking in the fractional method. Analysis of metals by the fractional method proceeds in two stages: first the interfering ions are removed, then the metal is detected with a reagent giving a colour or precipitate. Masking is based on converting interfering ions into a stable complex, changing the valency, and changing the pH. Demasking, on the other hand, is the release of the masked ion from the masking reagent.

Masking reagents and the ions they mask. Cyanides form complexes with Cu, Co, Fe, Ni, Zn, Cd, Hg and Ag ions; fluoride and phosphates mask Fe3+. Thiosulphates mask Ag, Pb, Cu and Fe ions, and thiourea masks Bi, Fe, Sb, Cd, Hg, Ag and Pb ions. Citric acid masks Bi, Cu, Fe, Sb, Cd, Hg and Ag ions, while tartaric acid masks Cu, Fe, Al, Bi, Cd, Hg, Pb and Zn ions.

Let us look at the example of masking Fe3+ with fluoride. In detecting Co2+ with ammonium thiocyanate, Fe3+ interferes: it forms blood-red Fe(CNS)3. Fluoride and phosphates are used to mask Fe3+: colourless stable complexes [FeF6]3- and [Fe(PO4)2]3- form. Phosphates and phosphoric acid in an acid medium form colourless complexes with Fe3+ ions. As a result, the red colour of Fe(CNS)3 does not appear.

Masking copper with cyanide proceeds in two stages: first Cu2+ is reduced, then a complex ion forms. First: CuSO4 + 2KCN → Cu(CN)2 + K2SO4. Second: 2Cu(CN)2 → 2CuCN + (CN)2. Third: CuCN + 3KCN → K3[Cu(CN)4]. Cyanides are poisonous: they cannot be added to an acid solution, because in acid volatile, toxic hydrogen cyanide forms. For this reason experiments with cyanides are carried out in a fume cupboard.

The "Boomerang" training. Students are divided into small groups and materials with the task are handed out; each group presents its view, and the groups ask and answer questions among themselves. Group I presents the methods of wet mineralisation of "metallic" poisons, their performance, advantages and disadvantages. Group II presents the methods of denitration of the mineralisate, their performance, advantages and disadvantages. Group III presents the methods of dry mineralisation of "metallic" poisons, their performance, advantages and disadvantages.

A practical situation, that is, case 8. During mineralisation the amount of black vapours increased. Task: to explain what phenomenon occurred, its cause and the solution, and to carry out the forensic chemical analysis. Columns of the answer table: type of problem, causes of origin and ways of resolving it.

The situational problem for the first group. The internal organs of a corpse were submitted for forensic chemical examination: liver, kidneys, stomach, brain, adipose tissue, lungs, and also blood, urine and hair. In a garage, beside a dead car mechanic who was found there, are two broken glass containers without labels. The liquid of the first container gave a positive result with potassium permanganate. The liquid of the second container gave a red colour with a solution of dithizone in chloroform at pH = 7.5-8; with 5% potassium iodide solution a yellow precipitate formed. Question: indicate the procedure for isolating the toxic substance from the internal organs of the corpse.

There are four review questions. First: what are the reasons for mineralisation, that is, destruction of a biological object; indicate its stages and characterise them. Second: how can one tell that the process is complete; what are the advantages and disadvantages of wet mineralisation? Third: what is the purpose of testing the mineralisate with a solution of diphenylamine in concentrated sulphuric acid? Fourth: what advantages does formaldehyde have as a denitrating agent compared with sodium sulphite and urea?

Safety and working procedure. The flask is fixed in the stand over the gas flame and heated carefully; a fume cupboard is listed among the necessary equipment. Nitric acid is added carefully, dropwise. The cooled mineralisate is carefully transferred into a beaker. In denitration a brown gas is sometimes evolved; white heavy vapours of sulphur(VI) oxide are also evolved.

Recording the result. The student who has finished the work, having had the correctness of the results confirmed by the instructor, writes a conclusion in the laboratory notebook. One of the expected outcomes is studying the appearance of the object containing metal compounds. At the end the mineralisate is diluted to 180 ml, boiled for 5 minutes and left until the next session.

There are four reaction tasks in the book. First: explain by chemical reactions the destruction of organic molecules by oxidants in mineralisation. Second: write the equation of the reaction for detecting oxidants in the mineralisate with a solution of diphenylamine in sulphuric acid. Third: write and explain the chemical equations of the reactions of denitration with formaldehyde and of removing excess formaldehyde. Fourth: characterise nitrosyl sulphuric acid from the chemical point of view and explain it on the basis of reactions.

There are three independent work tasks. The first is "Analysis of concepts", where the definition "Mineralisation is –" must be completed. The second is "Practical skill": to depict the mineralisation apparatus, that is, the Kjeldahl flask, stand and burner. The third is the "3x4" method: students are divided into groups of 3-4, the instructor asks questions, and the student reasons freely, gives a definition and draws a conclusion.
